nodes.title: CLIP Text Encode (Positive Prompt)
widgets_values: A man in a grey suit sits at a desk in a bright office, looking at the camera, speaking in English saying: "REPLACE WITH THE NEW LINE, ROUGHLY THE SAME LENGTH AS THE ORIGINAL."

# How to Prompt a Good Dub-It/Rephrase

This workflow supports both **dubbing** (translating speech into another language) and **rephrasing** (changing what the speaker says while keeping the same language). In both cases, the model will generate new lip movements and audio to match the text you provide.

## 1. Include the translated words in your prompt

The prompt should contain the translated words you want the speaker to say. The model will **not** translate it for you.

## 2. Use native script

Use the alphabet of the language you want the model to speak - for example, Cyrillic for Russian or Chinese characters for Chinese.

## 3. Single speaker only

The current LoRA supports only one speaker.

## 4. Match the length of the original for the best audio

Try to keep your translation close to the length of the original dialogue.

- **Too long** — The model might skip words.
- **Too short** — The output might sound slow and unnatural.

> **Tip:** Since there are many ways to say the same thing, play around with your wording until the length is right.

The `latent_downscale_factor` output from the IC-LoRA Loader is intentionally ignored. The Dub-It LoRA was trained with `reference_downscale_factor = 1` (full resolution), so no spatial downscaling of the reference is needed. For reference on handling other values, see `LTX-2.3_ICLoRA_Union_Control_Distilled.json`

# 🎬 LipSync Template · LTX-2.3 Dub-It

**What it does:** takes a clip of an actor speaking and makes them say a *new line*.
New lip movement **and** new audio are generated; the actor's voice is cloned from the clip's original audio.

> Two modes, toggled in **STEP 2b**:
> - **Text** (default): write the new line in the prompt; the voice is cloned from the clip.
> - **Recorded audio**: your recording is kept as-is and only the lips are regenerated to match it.

---

## ✅ Checklist before first run

1. **Custom nodes** (Manager → Install Custom Nodes):
   - `ComfyUI-LTXVideo` (Lightricks), **required**
   - `ComfyUI-KJNodes` (kijai): `GetImageSizeAndCount`
   - ComfyUI core must be **recent** (LTXV audio/video nodes are core)
2. **Models**, exact names and folders:

| File | models/ folder |
|---|---|
| `ltx-2.3-22b-dev-fp8.safetensors` (29 GB) | `checkpoints` |
| `ltx-2.3-22b-distilled-lora-384-1.1.safetensors` (7.6 GB) | `loras` |
| `ltx-2.3-22b-ic-lora-dubit-0.9.safetensors` (2.5 GB, **gated**) | `loras` |
| `ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1.safetensors` (1 GB) | `latent_upscale_models` |
| `gemma_3_12B_it_fp4_mixed.safetensors` (9.5 GB) | `text_encoders` |

3. **Hardware:** NVIDIA, 32 GB+ VRAM recommended (24 GB: set **S1 PIXELS** to 344064 and add decode tiles). Won't run on a Mac.
4. Put your clip in ComfyUI `input/` and select it in **STEP 2**.
5. Write the new line in **STEP 3**, then **Queue**.

## 🔁 Run order
STEP 1 → 7 left to right. You normally only touch **STEP 2** (clip), **STEP 3** (prompt), and maybe **S1 PIXELS** (Auto size) or **CROP TO FACE** (STEP 2c).

## STEP 1 · Models
- **Checkpoint**, **Audio VAE loader** and **Text Encoder loader** all point at the *same* checkpoint file. If you switch to the full bf16 `ltx-2.3-22b-dev.safetensors` (46 GB), change **all three**.
- **Distilled LoRA @ 0.5**: lets it run in ~8+3 steps. Leave as is.
- **Dub-It IC-LoRA @ 1.0**: the lipdub model. Try 0.8–1.0 if mouths look over-animated.
- Text encoder: `fp4_mixed` is smallest. If it errors or looks off on an older GPU, use `gemma_3_12B_it_fp8_scaled.safetensors`.
- Low on VRAM? Enable the **Gemma API** nodes in STEP 3 (needs an LTX API key) and drop the local text encoder.

## STEP 2 · Actor clip: what works best
- **One speaker**, face clearly visible, mouth not covered. Near-frontal is best.
- **Steady camera / shot**. Cut long footage into single shots of **~3–8 s** first (VRAM grows with length).
- The clip's **own audio is the voice reference**, so give it clean dialogue (no music bed).
- Frame count is snapped automatically to LTX's `8n+1` (e.g. 121 = 5 s @ 24 fps). FPS is taken from the clip.
- Keep frames at **4 MP or less** (e.g. 3240×1234, 2560×1440): bigger clips can run out of system RAM.
- **Sizes are automatic**: s1 follows the clip's shape (any aspect ratio) within the **S1 PIXELS** budget (Auto size group).

## STEP 3 · Writing the prompt
Format: **scene description + `speaking in <language> saying: "<exact words>"`**

```
A woman in a red jacket stands on a rainy street at night,
looking slightly off camera, speaking in French saying:
"Je t'avais dit de ne pas revenir ici."
```
- Write the words **yourself**. It won't translate. Use native script (Cyrillic, 中文…).
- Keep it **about as long as the original line**: too long → words skipped; too short → slow, drawn-out speech.
- Describe the actor/scene as it *is*. That helps it keep identity.
- Negative prompt is fine as is.

## STEP 4 · Preprocess (usually leave alone)
- `LTXVAudioVAEEncode` → `LTXVSetAudioRefTokens`: original audio = **voice to clone**.
- `LTXAddVideoICLoRAGuide`: original frames = **guide** (identity, motion, background).
- `LTXVEmptyLatentAudio`: the **new** audio is generated from scratch.
- `EmptyLTXVLatentVideo` width/height come from s1 (Auto size).

**🎙 Recorded audio mode** (STEP 2b on): **Switch A** feeds your recording to the encoder instead of the clip's audio, and **Switch B** swaps the empty audio latent for the *frozen* recording (`frozen_audio`, never denoised), so only the lips are generated.

## STEP 5 · Low-res pass
- Generates audio + lip motion together at s1 size.
- `ManualSigmas` is the distilled 8-step schedule. **Don't change it.**
- CFG = 1 (distilled). Seed is **fixed**: change it in `RandomNoise` for a different take.
- Iterate here: if the low-res result is wrong, the high-res one will be too. To preview faster, temporarily bypass STEP 6 and wire STEP 5's output to decode.

## STEP 6 · High-res pass
- Latent is upscaled **2×**, the guide is re-applied at **s2**, then refined in 3 steps.
- s2 is always exactly 2× s1 (Auto size).
- **VRAM tight?** Lower **S1 PIXELS**: 344064 (24 GB) or 225280 (previews).
- `LTXVCropGuides` removes the guide frames before decode. Leave it.

## STEP 7 · Decode & save
- Out of memory at the end? Raise the tile counts in `LTXVTiledVAEDecode` (e.g. 2×2 → 3×3 or 4×4).
- Output is an MP4 with the new audio at the source FPS, in `output/`.
- Recorded audio mode: **Switch C** puts your original recording on the MP4 instead of the decoded copy.
- Need the original background audio back? Mix it in your editor: the model only outputs the new speech track.

nodes.title: Switch B · Generate or freeze audio

widgets_values:
## STEP 2b · Recorded audio (optional)

Toggle **USE RECORDED AUDIO**:

- **false** (default): *Text mode.* The line in STEP 3 is spoken in a new take, voice cloned from the clip.
- **true**: *Audio mode.* Your recording is the soundtrack exactly as recorded. The model only regenerates the **lips** to match it.

**Audio mode tips**
- Upload the recording in **Load Recorded Audio** (wav, mp3, m4a, or a video file).
- In text mode leave it on `no_audio.wav` (a silent placeholder from `make lipsync-setup`): ComfyUI checks this node even when it's switched off.
- It's trimmed to the clip length from 0 s, so line it up with the clip before uploading.
- Still write the **transcript** in the STEP 3 prompt (`speaking in English saying: "..."`). It helps the mouth shapes.
- Clean speech, one speaker, no music.
- Experimental: Lightricks built Dub-It for text mode. Check the sync on every take.

nodes.title: Switch D · Full frame or face crop

widgets_values:
## STEP 2c · Crop to face (optional)

Turn **CROP TO FACE** on for wide shots: the model's resolution then goes to the face instead of the whole frame, so lips come out sharper. The saved output is the face crop.

**Previews** (green groups, temp files only, nothing extra saved):
- *Face detection + crop box*: detected face mask in green, crop window in red, on the original clip.
- *Face crop (model input)*: exactly what the model sees.
- *Result pasted onto original* (next to STEP 7): the dubbed face crop blended back into the full frame.
With CROP TO FACE off they just show the clip / the normal result, and face detection doesn't run.

- **FACE ZOOM**: crop size as a multiple of the face. **1.8** = head, hair, chin and top of the shoulders. Lower = tighter.
- **TRACKING SMOOTHING**: how fast the crop follows the head. Lower = steadier (0.2 to 0.5).
- Black edges in the result mean the crop hit the frame edge: lower FACE ZOOM a little.
- **Huge clips run out of RAM** (system RAM, not VRAM): frames are held as 32-bit floats, ~105 MB each at 4804×1830. Export a copy at **4 MP or less** first (e.g. 3240×1234). `make lipsync-test` does this for you.
- One face per shot. Frames where the face is missed are filled in from neighbouring frames.
- Needs `models/detection/mediapipe_face_fp32.safetensors` (`make lipsync-setup` downloads it).

## Auto size

**S1 PIXELS** is the only size knob: s1 width × height for the first pass. The shape follows your clip (or the face crop) and s2 is always 2× s1.

| S1 PIXELS | 16:9 s1 → s2 | GPU |
|---|---|---|
| 522240 | 960×544 → 1920×1088 | 32 GB+ |
| 344064 | 768×448 → 1536×896 | 24 GB |
| 225280 | 640×352 → 1280×704 | previews |
